title: Never, nothing, no one
description: Say never, no longer, nothing, no one, only and neither…nor.

guide.summary: Beyond ne…pas, French has a word for never, no longer, nothing, no one, only and neither…nor. This topic teaches which word to pick, where to put it, and what it does to the article after it.

sections.title: Which word replaces pas?
sections.text: Ne stays in front of the conjugated verb and becomes n’ before a vowel or a silent h. The second word says what kind of negative you mean, and it takes the place of pas: the two are never used together.

rows: Je ne bois que du thé.
Je n’aime ni le thé ni le café.

steps: Decide what you are denying: a time, a thing, a person, or a choice between items.
Keep ne (n’ before a vowel) in front of the conjugated verb.
Put the matching word after the verb and delete pas.
watch: Two negatives never stack: pas rien and pas jamais do not exist.
In speech ne is often dropped (je sais rien); written French keeps it.
Personne here means no one; une personne (a person) is a different, positive word.

sections.title: What happens to the article after it?
sections.text: After a true negative the indefinite and partitive articles shrink to de (d’ before a vowel), exactly as after pas. Le, la and les never change. Ne…que keeps everything; ni…ni deletes the article instead.
steps: Say the sentence in the positive first and look at the article it uses.
If it is le, la or les, leave it alone.
If it is un, une, des, du, de la or de l’, replace it with de after jamais or plus, and use d’ before a vowel.

examples.fr: Je ne mange jamais de viande.
Il ne regarde jamais la télé.

watch: Des never survives a true negative: jamais des légumes is wrong.
Je ne mange plus de pain means I no longer eat bread; without ne, je mange plus de pain can mean I eat more bread.

sections.title: Where does it go in the passé composé?
sections.text: Ne goes in front of the auxiliary. The second word takes the slot pas would take, between the auxiliary and the participle — except personne, which waits until the verb is finished.

rows: between the auxiliary and the participle
between the auxiliary and the participle
Je n’ai jamais vu ce film.
between the auxiliary and the participle
between the auxiliary and the participle

steps: Put ne (n’) in front of avoir or être.
Jamais, plus and rien: slot them straight after the auxiliary, before the participle.
Personne: keep the auxiliary and the participle together and put it after them.

examples.fr: Je n’ai jamais vu ce film.
examples.en: I have never seen this film.

watch: Je n’ai mangé jamais is the classic slip: jamais belongs before the participle.
Never squeeze personne between the auxiliary and the participle.
The article still shrinks: je n’ai jamais mangé de sushis.

sections.title: Only: ne…que
sections.text: Ne…que limits instead of denying: it means only. Nothing in the sentence is negated, so the article stays as it was.

rows: que goes right before the word it limits
Il ne mange que des légumes.
keep the article of the positive sentence
Je ne bois que du thé.
only — a restriction, never a denial

steps: Ask whether the sentence denies something or limits it to one thing; only is a limit.
Put que immediately in front of the limited word, and qu’ before a vowel.
Leave the article exactly as a positive sentence would have it.

examples.fr: Je ne bois que du thé.
Il ne travaille que le samedi.

watch: Ne…que never takes de: que de pain is wrong.
Seulement says the same thing, but this topic practises ne…que.
Move que and you move the limit: il ne boit que de l’eau le matin limits the drink, not the time.

sections.title: Neither…nor: ne…ni…ni
sections.text: Ni goes before each item and replaces both pas and the linking et or ou. Indefinite and partitive articles disappear entirely; definite ones stay.

rows: dropped: je n’ai ni frère ni sœur
dropped: nous ne prenons ni lait ni sucre
kept: je n’aime ni le thé ni le café
never used: ni…ni has already replaced it

steps: Take pas out: ni already makes the sentence negative.
Put ni in front of every item, the first one included.
Delete un, une, des, du and de la; keep le, la and les.

examples.fr: Elle n’a ni chien ni chat.
examples.en: She has neither a dog nor a cat.

examples.fr: Je n’aime ni le thé ni le café.
examples.en: I like neither tea nor coffee.

watch: Ni…ou does not exist: the same word is repeated before each item.
Forgetting the first ni (nous ne prenons lait ni sucre) is the usual slip.

sections.title: When nothing or no one is the subject
sections.text: Rien and personne can be the subject of the sentence. They come first, ne still stands in front of the verb, and pas is not used.
steps: Start the sentence with the negative subject.
Put ne (n’) before the verb, as in any negative sentence.
Leave pas out, and keep the verb in the singular.
watch: Personne ne sait pas has one negative too many.
The verb stays singular: rien ne change, never rien ne changent.

sections.title: One-word answers
sections.text: A short answer has no verb, so there is nothing for ne to stand in front of. The negative word answers on its own.
steps: Check whether your answer contains a verb.
If it has none, give the negative word by itself.
Add neither ne nor pas.

examples.fr: — Tu fais du sport ? — Non, jamais !
examples.en: — Do you do sport? — No, never!

watch: Ne personne and pas jamais are impossible: both words need a verb.
Match the question word: qui is answered by personne, que by rien.

Un, une, des, du, de la and de l’ all shrink to de, and to d’ before a vowel.

Keep ne before the verb and put that word straight after the verb.
Remove pas: it is never used together with these words.
Find the auxiliary (avoir or être) and put ne in front of it.
Slide the negative word into the slot pas would take, right after the auxiliary.
Finish with the past participle, and shrink the article after it if there is one.
Put ne (n’) in front of the auxiliary.
Keep the auxiliary and the past participle side by side, with nothing between them.
Put the word for no one after the participle, where the object would be.
Check that the sentence limits rather than denies: only means a limit.
Put que immediately before the limited word, qu’ before a vowel.
Keep the article the positive sentence would use, and add no pas.
Take pas out of the sentence.
Put ni before each item, including the first one.
Drop un, une, des, du and de la; keep le, la and les.
Put the negative subject at the front of the sentence.
Add ne (n’) before the verb.
Use no pas, and keep the verb singular.
Check whether your answer has a verb in it.
With no verb, reply with the negative word alone.
Match it to the question word: who, what, or how often.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word that completes the sentence.
exercises.hint: Jamais works like pas: the article after it changes.
exercises.feedback: Du and de la do not stay after ne…jamais.
exercises.explanation: After ne…jamais, du, de la, un, une and des become de: je ne mange jamais de viande.

mistakes.why: These are the partitive articles of a positive sentence (je mange de la viande). A true negative flattens them to one short form, exactly as ne…pas does.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite with ne…jamais: I never watch TV in the evening.
exercises.source: Je regarde la télé le soir.
answers: Je ne regarde jamais la télé le soir.

alternatives.answer: Je regarde jamais la télé le soir.
alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne before the verb.

exercises.hint: Jamais takes the place of pas, right after the verb.
exercises.feedback: Put ne before regarde and jamais after it. Does la change?
exercises.explanation: Ne…jamais surrounds the verb like ne…pas, and la stays unchanged.

answers: Je ne regarde pas jamais la télé le soir.
mistakes.why: This keeps pas and adds the word for never on top of it. One sentence takes one negative word after ne.

answers: Je ne regarde jamais de télé le soir.
mistakes.why: You shrank the article, but la télé is definite: le, la and les never change after a negative.

answers: Je ne jamais regarde la télé le soir.
Jamais je ne regarde la télé le soir.
mistakes.why: The negative word does not go in front of the verb in a simple tense; only ne does. Everything else follows the conjugated verb.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: She never takes the bus (le bus).
answers: Elle ne prend jamais le bus.

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne before the verb.

exercises.hint: Never is ne…jamais around the verb.
exercises.feedback: Check that ne comes before prend and jamais right after it.
exercises.explanation: Ne…jamais surrounds prend. The definite article le does not change.

answers: Elle ne prend pas jamais le bus.
mistakes.why: Pas is still there. The word meaning never takes its place instead of joining it.

answers: Elle ne prend jamais de bus.
mistakes.why: Le bus is a definite article and stays as it is; only un, une, des, du and de la shrink after a negative.

answers: Elle ne jamais prend le bus.
mistakes.why: Only ne goes before the conjugated verb. The second negative word follows the verb in the present tense.

exercises.instruction: Fill the blank with the word for never.
exercises.hint: Ne is already there. Which word pairs with it to mean never?
exercises.feedback: The word you need means never, not not.
exercises.explanation: Ne…jamais means never: vous ne faites jamais de sport.

mistakes.why: Pas is the plain negative: vous ne faites pas de sport just says you don’t do sport, with nothing about how often.
Plus means no longer: it says you used to do sport and stopped, not that you do none at any time.
Rien stands for a thing and personne for a human being. The blank needs a word about frequency, not an empty object.
Encore means still or again, which is positive: it would say you do sport once more.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.source: Il ne mange jamais des légumes.
answers: Il ne mange jamais de légumes.
exercises.hint: Jamais changes the article after it, just as pas does.
exercises.feedback: Des does not stay after ne…jamais.
exercises.explanation: After ne…jamais, des becomes de: il ne mange jamais de légumes.

answers: Il ne mange jamais des légumes.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence as it stands. Des is a positive-sentence article and cannot survive after a negative.

answers: Il ne mange pas jamais des légumes.
mistakes.why: Adding pas creates two negative words and leaves the article untouched, so the sentence is worse, not fixed.

answers: Il ne mange jamais les légumes.
mistakes.why: Les is not the shrunken article; it changes the meaning to those particular vegetables. The partitive has to be reduced, not swapped for a definite article.

exercises.instruction: Choose the word that completes the sentence.
exercises.hint: Plus changes the article after it, like pas. Argent begins with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: De l’ does not stay after ne…plus.
exercises.explanation: After ne…plus, de l’ becomes de, and de becomes d’ before argent.

mistakes.why: De l’ is the article of a positive sentence (j’ai de l’argent). A true negative reduces it.
The reduction is right, but argent begins with a vowel, and this full form cannot stand in front of a vowel: it has to be elided.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
answers: Je ne mange plus de viande.

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne before the verb. Without ne, this can also be read as I eat more meat.

exercises.hint: Not anymore is ne…plus. Check the article after it.
exercises.feedback: De la does not stay after ne…plus.
exercises.explanation: Ne…plus surrounds mange, and de la becomes de: je ne mange plus de viande.

answers: Je ne mange plus de la viande.
mistakes.why: De la is the positive-sentence article and does not survive a negative; it has to be reduced.

answers: Je ne mange pas plus de viande.
mistakes.why: With pas kept, the sentence reads I don’t eat more meat: a comparison, not a habit that stopped.

answers: Je ne mange jamais de viande.
mistakes.why: Jamais means never, at any time. Anymore says you did it before and stopped.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite with ne…plus: he no longer lives in Paris.

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne before the verb. Without ne, plus can be misread as more.

exercises.hint: Habite starts with a silent h, so ne shortens.
exercises.feedback: Check the elision before habite and the position of plus.
exercises.explanation: Ne becomes n’ before the silent h, and plus follows the verb: il n’habite plus à Paris.

answers: Il ne habite plus à Paris.
mistakes.why: Habite starts with a silent h, so ne cannot keep its e in front of it; it must be elided.

answers: Il n’habite pas plus à Paris.
mistakes.why: Pas is still in the sentence, and pas plus reads as not more: it becomes a comparison instead of a change over time.
Jamais says he has never lived there at all, which loses the idea that he lived there before.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: We don’t have any bread left. Leave the extra tile unused.
exercises.source: We don’t have any bread left.
exercises.hint: No more is ne…plus, and the article after it changes.
exercises.feedback: Du does not stay after ne…plus.
exercises.explanation: Nous n’avons plus de pain: du becomes de after ne…plus.

mistakes.why: Du is the leftover tile from a positive sentence. A true negative reduces the partitive article.
Without ne this reads as we have more bread, the opposite of what you mean. Written French keeps ne in front of the verb.

exercises.instruction: Fill the blank with the word for no longer.
exercises.hint: Ne is already there. Which word pairs with it to mean no longer?
exercises.feedback: The word you need means no longer, not never.
exercises.explanation: Ne…plus means no longer: ils ne travaillent plus ici.

mistakes.why: Pas only makes the sentence negative: they don’t work here, with nothing about a change from before.
Jamais means never: it says they have never worked here at all, not that they used to and stopped.
Rien stands for a thing, and ici is a place: there is no object missing from this sentence.
Encore means still, which keeps them at work: it says the opposite of what you want.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right form.
exercises.source: Il fait noir : je ne vois ____.
exercises.hint: Rien replaces pas. It is never used with pas.
exercises.feedback: Only one word goes after the verb with ne here.
exercises.explanation: Ne…rien means nothing. Rien takes the place of pas, so the two are not combined.

mistakes.why: Both keep pas alongside a second negative word. The word meaning nothing already takes the place of pas, so only one of them appears after the verb.

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne before the verb.

exercises.hint: Not anyone is ne…personne around the verb.
exercises.feedback: Do not add pas: personne already makes the sentence negative.
exercises.explanation: Ne…personne surrounds connais: je ne connais personne ici.

answers: Je ne connais pas personne ici.
mistakes.why: Pas and a second negative word cannot share the same verb; the word for no one already carries the negation.

answers: Je ne connais pas quelqu’un ici.
mistakes.why: This is a word-for-word copy of not anyone. French negates the person itself instead of putting pas in front of quelqu’un.
Rien covers things. You are talking about human beings here, which needs the other word.

exercises.instruction: Fill the blank with the word for nothing.
exercises.hint: Ne is already there. Which word pairs with it to mean nothing?
exercises.feedback: The word you need means nothing, not no one.
exercises.explanation: Ne…rien means nothing: il ne dit rien ce matin.

mistakes.why: Pas only makes the verb negative: he isn’t saying. The blank has to name the empty content of what he says.
Personne means no one, a human being. What someone says is a thing, not a person.
Jamais is about frequency: it would say he never speaks in the mornings, not that his words add up to zero.
Plus means no longer, a change over time. The blank is the object of dit, not a word about when.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: She isn’t waiting for anyone. Leave the extra tile unused.
exercises.hint: Attendre takes a direct object: no word for for is needed.
exercises.feedback: Personne already carries the negation, so pas is not used.
exercises.explanation: Ne…personne surrounds attend, and ne elides before the vowel: elle n’attend personne.

mistakes.why: The pas tile is the distractor: the word at the end already makes the sentence negative, so pas has no place.
Ne has been left out. That happens in casual speech, but a written sentence keeps it in front of the verb.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error.
exercises.hint: Rien takes the place of pas.
exercises.feedback: There is one negative word too many.
exercises.explanation: Ne…rien already means nothing, so pas is removed: nous ne voulons rien.

mistakes.why: This is the sentence as it stands: it still has two negative words after ne, and only one is allowed.
You removed the wrong word. The sentence now just says we don’t want to, and the idea of zero things is gone.
You removed ne instead of pas. Ne is the part that must stay in front of the verb in writing.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right form.
exercises.hint: In the passé composé, rien goes where pas would go.
exercises.feedback: Rien does not follow the participle.
exercises.explanation: Like pas, rien goes between the auxiliary and the participle: je n’ai rien vu.

mistakes.why: One puts the negative word after the participle, the other in front of the auxiliary. In the passé composé it takes the same slot as pas: after the auxiliary and before the participle.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite with ne…rien: she ate nothing.

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne before the verb.

exercises.hint: Rien goes between the auxiliary and the participle.
exercises.feedback: Put ne before the auxiliary and check where rien goes.
exercises.explanation: In the passé composé, ne…rien surrounds the auxiliary: elle n’a rien mangé.

mistakes.why: Only the word for no one goes after the participle. A thing that is missing takes the slot of pas, inside the verb.
Pas is still there, so the sentence has two negative words; keeping both would even cancel the meaning.
Nothing goes between ne and the auxiliary: ne sits directly in front of avoir.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French.
exercises.source: I have never seen this film.
answers: Je n’ai jamais vu ce film.

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne before the verb.

exercises.hint: Use the passé composé. Jamais goes where pas would go.
exercises.feedback: Jamais sits between the auxiliary and the participle.
exercises.explanation: Ne…jamais surrounds the auxiliary ai: je n’ai jamais vu ce film.

answers: Je n’ai vu jamais ce film.
mistakes.why: The negative word has fallen behind the participle. Only the word for no one does that; the others stay inside the verb.

answers: Je n’ai pas jamais vu ce film.
mistakes.why: Pas is kept as well, which gives two negative words for one verb.

answers: Je ne vois jamais ce film.
mistakes.why: This is the present tense: I never watch this film. The English have seen calls for the passé composé.

exercises.instruction: Write téléphoner in the passé composé with ne…plus.
exercises.hint: The auxiliary is avoir. Plus goes where pas would go.
exercises.feedback: Write the auxiliary, the negation and the participle in the right order.
exercises.explanation: Ne…plus surrounds the auxiliary a, and the participle follows: elle n’a plus téléphoné.

mistakes.why: The negative word has slipped behind the participle. Only the word for no one stands there; the others sit inside the verb.
Ne must touch the auxiliary: nothing is allowed between them.
This is the ordinary negative, she didn’t call. It loses the idea that the calls stopped after a certain point.
Téléphoner builds its passé composé with avoir, not être.

exercises.instruction: Fix the word order.
exercises.source: Je n’ai mangé jamais de sushis.
answers: Je n’ai jamais mangé de sushis.
exercises.hint: In the passé composé, jamais does not follow the participle.
exercises.feedback: Move jamais so it sits right after the auxiliary.
exercises.explanation: Jamais goes between the auxiliary and the participle: je n’ai jamais mangé.

answers: Je n’ai mangé jamais de sushis.
mistakes.why: This is the sentence as it stands, with the negative word stranded after the participle.

answers: Je n’ai jamais mangé des sushis.
mistakes.why: The order is fixed, but des cannot stay after a negative: the partitive article has to shrink.

answers: Je ne jamais ai mangé de sushis.
mistakes.why: Nothing may stand between ne and the auxiliary; the negative word belongs on the other side of ai.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right form.
exercises.hint: Personne does not follow the rule for pas, jamais and rien in the passé composé.
exercises.feedback: Personne goes after the whole verb.
exercises.explanation: Unlike rien, personne goes after the past participle: je n’ai vu personne.

mistakes.why: These treat the word like pas, rien or jamais and push it inside the verb. The word for a human being is the exception: it waits until the participle is done.

exercises.instruction: Replace ses amis with personne: she invited no one.

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne before the verb.

exercises.hint: Personne takes the place of the object, after the participle.

exercises.explanation: In the passé composé, personne follows the participle: elle n’a invité personne.

mistakes.why: This is the slot pas takes, and the word for a human being is precisely the one that does not use it.
Pas is still in the sentence, which gives two negative words for one verb.

answers: Elle n’a pas invité ses amis.
mistakes.why: This only denies that she invited her friends; the object has to be replaced by the negative word, not kept.

exercises.instruction: Translate into French using the passé composé.

alternatives.message: That is common in casual speech, but written French keeps ne before the verb.

exercises.hint: Personne goes in a different place from pas in the passé composé.
exercises.feedback: Personne comes after the past participle, not before it.
exercises.explanation: Ne goes before the auxiliary, and personne goes after the participle: il n’a appelé personne.

mistakes.why: That is where pas, rien and jamais go. The word for a human being comes later, once the verb is complete.
Pas is kept alongside a second negative word; only one of them belongs after ne.
Rien stands for a thing. Anyone means a human being, which needs the other word.

exercises.instruction: Fix the word order.

exercises.explanation: Personne follows the past participle: tu n’as rencontré personne.

answers: Tu n’as personne rencontré à la fête.

answers: Tu n’as pas rencontré personne à la fête.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: I didn’t hear anyone. Leave the extra tile unused.

exercises.explanation: Je n’ai entendu personne: ne before the auxiliary, personne after the participle.

mistakes.why: The pas tile is the distractor: the last word already makes the sentence negative.

exercises.instruction: Choose the article.
exercises.hint: Ne…que means only. It is a restriction, not a true negation.
exercises.feedback: The article does not become de after ne…que.
exercises.explanation: Ne…que keeps the article: je ne bois que du thé.

exercises.feedback: Check the elision of que before un, and keep the article.
exercises.explanation: Ne…que keeps un: je n’ai qu’un frère.

mistakes.why: Que cannot keep its e in front of a vowel; un begins with one, so the word has to be shortened.
Adding pas flips the meaning to not only one brother, which says you have more than one.

exercises.instruction: Rewrite with ne…que: he eats only vegetables.

alternatives.message: That is correct French, but this exercise practises ne…que.

exercises.hint: Que goes right before des légumes, and des stays.
exercises.feedback: Ne…que is not a real negation, so the article does not change.
exercises.explanation: Ne…que keeps the article: il ne mange que des légumes.

answers: Il ne mange que de légumes.
mistakes.why: You reduced the article as after a true negative. Restricting the choice does not deny the vegetables, so the article stays whole.

answers: Il ne mange pas que des légumes.

Le cannot stand in front of a word beginning with a vowel: it would have to be elided too.
Seulement means only on its own, but the sentence already began with ne, so the blank must be the second half of that pair.

answers: Nous ne prenons ni de lait ni de sucre.

exercises.instruction: Choose the right short answer.
exercises.hint: In a short answer without a verb, ne is not used.
exercises.feedback: Ne needs a verb. A one-word answer does not have one.

mistakes.why: Ne needs a verb to stand in front of, and pas needs one too. A one-word reply has no verb, so the negative word answers alone.

exercises.explanation: Jamais can be used alone as a short answer: Non, jamais !

mistakes.why: Both drag a second word into a reply that has no verb. Ne only works in front of a verb, and pas cannot stack with another negative.

Personne answers the question qui (who). This question asks what you bought, so the reply must stand for a thing.
